READING PASSAGE 2
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2
on pages 6 and 7.
Nature’s numbers
A We live in a universe of patterns. Every night the stars move in circles across the sky.
The seasons cycle at yearly intervals. No two snowflakes are ever the same, but they all
have sixfold symmetry. Intricate trains of waves march across the oceans. Colored arcs
of light adorn the sky in the form of rainbows, and a bright circular halo sometimes
surrounds the moon on winter nights. Spherical drops of water fall from clouds. Human
mind and culture have developed a formal system of thought for recognizing, classifying
and exploiting patterns. We call it mathematics. By using mathematics to organize and
systemize our ideas about patterns, we have discovered a great secret: nature’s
patterns are not just there to be admired, but are vital clues to the rules that govern
natural processes.
B Four hundred years ago, the German astronomer Johannes Kepler wrote a small book,
The Six-Cornered Snowflake, as a gift to his sponsor. In it he argued that any one
snowflake must be made by the packing together of tiny identical units. Kepler
performed no experiments; he simply thought very hard about various bits and pieces
of common knowledge. His main evidence was the sixfold symmetry of snowflakes,
which is a natural consequence of regular packing. If you place a large number of
identical coins on a table and try to fit them together as closely as possible, you get an
arrangement in which every coin is surrounded by six others arranged in a perfect
hexagon.
C There is much beauty in nature’s clues, and we can all recognize it without any
mathematical training. There is beauty, too, in the mathematical stories that start from
the clues and allow us to deduce the underlying rules and regularities, but it is a
different kind of beauty, applying to ideas rather than things. Patterns possess utility as
well as beauty. Once we have learned to recognize a background pattern, oddities
suddenly stand out. Against the circling background of stars, a small number that move
quite differently beg to be singled out for us to focus on. The ancient Greeks called
them planetes, meaning ‘wanderers’, a term retained in our word ‘planet’. It took a lot
longer to understand the patterns of planetary motion than it did to work out why stars
seem to move in nightly circles, but the planets were clues to the rules behind gravity.
D_ The simplest mathematical objects are numbers, and the simplest of nature’s patterns
are numerical. The phases of the moon — apparently varying its form from new to full
and back — make a complete cycle every twenty-eight days; people have two legs;
insects have six; starfish have five arms (or ten, eleven or seventeen depending on the
species). A very curious pattern indeed occurs in the petals of flowers: in nearly all
flowers, the number of petals is one that occurs in the strange sequence 3, 5, 8, 13, 21,
34, 55, 89, known as the Fibonacci numbers, in which each number is obtained by
adding the two previous numbers together.
E This sort of numerology is the easiest, and consequently the most dangerous method
for finding patterns. It is easy because anybody can do it, and dangerous for the same

reason. Here is a case in point: Kepler was fascinated with mathematical patterns in
nature, and devoted his life to looking for them in the behavior of the planets. He
devised a simple and tidy theory for the existence of precisely six planets, which we
realize today is inaccurate. He also discovered a very strange pattern relating the orbital
period of a planet — the time it takes to go once around the sun — to its distance from
the sun. Which of these numerological observations was more significant? The passage
of time has proved that it is the second one: Kepler’s neat and tidy theory for the
number of planets has long been buried without a trace.
There are also geometrical patterns. For example, many of nature’s patterns are based
on the circle. These include the rainbow, the human eye, and the ripples on a pond.
Ripples are particularly interesting, as the flow of fluids provides a vast supply of
patterns — waves in groups surging towards a beach in parallel lines, waves in a
V-shape behind a boat, and spiral whirlpools. There are also wave patterns on land.
The most striking mathematical landscapes on Earth are to be found in the great sand
oceans of the Arabian and Sahara deserts. Even when the wind blows in one direction,
semicircular sand dunes form, sometimes lined up in parallel lines like ocean waves,
and sometimes broken up into other patterns.
We are still learning to recognize new kinds of pattern. Only within the last few decades
has humanity become aware of the two types of pattern now known as fractals and
chaos. Fractals are geometric shapes that repeat their structure on ever finer scales.
Many of nature’s shapes, including river networks, trees, and very possibly the way that
matter is distributed throughout the entire universe, belong to this category of pattern;
chaos is the dynamic process that brings them into existence.
The more elusive of nature’s patterns are now beginning to reveal their secrets.
Researchers are even using these patterns in a trial that will hopefully allow them to
steer artificial satellites to new destinations with far less fuel than anybody once
thought possible. It is also helping to avoid wear on the wheels of locomotives, to
improve the effectiveness of heart pacemakers and to manage forests and fisheries.
Most important of all, it is giving us a deeper vision of the universe in which we live,
and of our own place in it.
